content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here are a few tips:

1. Mix up departments or teams: Rather than having people from the same department or team sitting together, mix them up throughout the room. This way, people who might not normally interact during the workday have the chance to get to know each other.

2. Use ice breaker questions: Consider putting a printed card on each table with an ice breaker question or two. This can serve as a conversation starter and encourage people to mingle.

3. Create a mix of personalities: As much as possible, mix outgoing people with those who may be more reserved. This way, the outgoing people can draw out the quieter people and help everyone get to know each other.

4. Consider the seating arrangements: Round tables encourage conversation, while banquet-style tables might make it harder for people to talk across the table.

5. Keep it balanced: Make sure that each table has a mix of men and women, ages, and job titles. This helps ensure that everyone has the opportunity to meet and engage with people they might not normally interact with.

Overall, the goal is to create a seating plan that encourages conversation and mingling, rather than just keeping people in their cliques. content:Speaker assistant says: How to Build a Robotic Bird Using Arduino

Are you interested in building a fun, yet challenging robot that can mimic the movements of a bird? Well, look no further! In this step-by-step how-to guide, we will walk you through the process of building a robotic bird using Arduino. This guide is suitable for beginners and advanced hobbyists alike. With the help of this guide, you will learn how to build a robotic bird from scratch using a few essential materials, programming steps, and the necessary tools.

Materials You Will Need:

- Arduino Uno Board
- 2 Servo Motors
- Prototype PCB Board
- Jumper Wires
- Polymer Battery (3.7V)
- Battery Holder
- Breadboard
- Male-to-Female Connector Wires
- Soldering Iron
- Soldering Wire
- Wire cutters
- Screwdriver
- Pliers

Step 1: Design Your Robotic Bird

Before you start building your robotic bird, you will need to design it. You can use basic bird shapes as a template, or you can design a completely unique bird shape using any design tool of your choice. Once you have your design, you will need to map out the areas where the servomotors will be placed.

Step 2: Prepare the Servo Motors

Take the two servos and connect them to the breadboard. Connect the ground wire (usually black) of each servo motor to the ground rail on the breadboard. Then connect the positive wire (usually red) of each servo motor to the 5V rail on the breadboard.

Step 3: Connect the Servo Motors to the Arduino Uno Board

Connect the left wing servo to pin 9 and the right wing servo to pin 10 of the Arduino Uno board. Make sure the signal wire (usually yellow) of each servo motor is connected to the correct pin on the Arduino board.

Step 4: Prepare the PCB Board

Use pliers to cut the PCB board to the desired shape and size of your bird. If you need holes in your PCB board, use a drill to create them. Now, solder the positive and negative wires of the servo motors to the PCB board where mapped earlier.

Step 5: Mount the Servo Motors and PCB Board

Use screws/nuts and bolts to attach the servo motors to the PCB board. Be sure to mount the servo motors in such a way that their moving arms can freely move up and down. Make sure the PCB board is also secured to the frame of the bird.

Step 6: Connect the Servo Motors and PCB Board to the Arduino Uno Board

Using male-to-female connector wires, connect the servo motors and PCB board to the Arduino Uno board. You can use a breadboard to help manage the connections, but make sure the connections are secure and firm.

Step 7: Power Up Your Robotic Bird

Connect the battery and battery holder to the Arduino board. The Polymer battery should be connected using the ground and positive wires respectively. After ensuring that all the connections are tight and secure, power up the Arduino board and watch your robotic bird come to life.

Step 8: Program Your Robotic Bird

It's now time to program your robotic bird. First, download and install the Arduino IDE on your computer. Then, connect your Arduino board to your computer and begin programming. The code should instruct the servo motors to move up and down in a synchronized manner, creating the desired flapping motion.

Step 9: Test Your Robotic Bird

After programming, upload the code to the Arduino board and test your robotic bird. If the bird is not flapping well, adjust the speed of the motors until the bird flaps correctly. In addition, you can experiment with different movements to give your bird unique characteristics.

Conclusion

Building a robotic bird may sound complicated, but with these simple steps, you can create an amazing bird that moves just like the real thing. Remember to be creative and experiment with different movements and designs. Just enjoy the process and have fun building your robotic bird. Good luck! context:This guide provides a step-by-step instructional overview for beginners and hobbyists on constructing a functional robotic bird using an Arduino Uno board, servo motors, and essential hardware components. keywords: robotic bird, Arduino, servo motors tags: maker_hobbies, programming_steps, hardware_assembly

content:Speaker user says: Are you using Instagram for your business or struggling to get to grips with how it works? With over 300 million users (70% outside the US) Instagram is definitely a social media platform to be exploited. Here are my top tips to boost your followers and increase engagement.
Research has shown that images with faces are the most engaging, attracting 35% more likes than images without. How simple is it to take advantage of that and get extra exposure for your brand and business! Use Instagram to introduce the people behind your business. Like other social media platforms, Instagram is a great way to express your brand less formally than your website or through more traditional communication channels. Share photographs of what goes on behind the scenes, who is responsible for dispatching the order a customer has placed, who customers will speak to when they have a query, new starters, the office dog and so on. If you can tell a story through your images, even better. Images of this type will convey the personality behind your brand and encourage a more emotional connection, an important element in creating brand fans.
Posting original content regularly is important, but you can increase your Instagram activity by paying attention to what your followers are posting. Like and share images posted by your followers, particularly ones that feature or refer to your products/services. It’s a kind of ‘you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours’ approach that should encourage more of your followers to share similar photos with you. And it also provides a different angle to how your business is presented. Always make sure you credit whoever posted the image by tagging them in your caption.
Creating a branded hashtag is also a good strategy. Encourage your followers to use it themselves, it will increase engagement and improve your visibility on Instagram in one fell swoop. Very generic hashtags, such as #handbag or #design, don’t work because there are simply too many other images with the same hashtag. Try instead to find something more unique that relates to your particular theme or business. Similarly, using too many hashtags gets messy, as well as smacking of desperation to build a following, so restrain yourself and concentrate on 2-3 hashtags that are totally relevant.
We all know that calls to action are essential in marketing, so why not use the same approach when you post an image on Instagram. Asking your followers what they think about an image is a great way of engaging with them and starting a 2-way conversation.
If you’ve done your hashtag homework well you will have discovered users that have a large amount of followers – they may well be Instagram influencers that are relevant to your business and therefore worth connecting with. Engage with them and start to build a relationship, making connections can often lead to interesting developments.
Consistency is everything. A flurry of activity followed by weeks of nothing posted will not foster a loyal following. Decide how many posts you can commit to per week and stick to it. It will also encourage you to be more discerning about what you post – quality is always preferable to quantity – and your followers will be grateful for that.

content:Speaker user says: Can you describe the differences in fashion between Elizabeth of York and her daughter-in-law Catherine of Aragon, as evidenced by their portraits and other visual representations?: When I tell people that I must turn to funerary art (monuments and brasses) to document early Tudor garb, they often ask why I do not use painted images such as portraits and illuminations. I answer that I would, if only there were any such sources for me to consult. Because of the excellent and numerous portraits created by Hans Holbein the Younger at the court of Henry VIII, people frequently assume that portraiture from the reign of Henry VII must exist as well. Unfortunately, little was apparently commissioned and even less remains.
The best collection of Tudor portraits is at the National Portrait Gallery and excellently documented online. Unfortunately, most of the portraits they have of the early Tudor era are copies from the late 16th-18th centuries. The oldest portraits they own are of men: Henry VII from 1505 and Henry VIII circa 1520. There are also several original paintings of Henry VIII from later in his life. Even the huge cartoon by Holbein of the Whitehall Mural only shows the half with the kings, not the queens.
The second best collection is supposed to be that at Hever Castle, Anne Boleyn's childhood home. I have not yet visited it, but the curator who answered my email told me that a 1509 portrait of Arthur, Prince of Wales (Henry VIII's deceased older brother and Catherine of Aragon's first husband) is the only portrait they have painted before 1520. Their other portraits of early Tudor nobility are copies made well after the sitter's lifetime.
The portrait of Elizabeth of York that I know so well is from the late sixteenth century. I find the text on the NPG page describing it frustrating but I've even written to verify that I understand it correctly, and "oil on panel, late 16th century (circa 1500)" means that the painting they have is from the late 16th century, but it is based on a (now lost) portrait from circa 1500. However, it is a starting point, and gives clues as to the neckline (square), gown closure (front), sleeve shape (tapering to fit the arm, with a fur cuff at the wrist). These details match what I see frequently on brasses. The headdress is difficult to interpret, being black against a dark background. An earlier version (1502-1550) of this same portrait is on display at Hampton Court Palace, as is the painting of the Family of Henry VII with St. George and the Dragon, dated 1503-1509. The former suffers from the same black-veil-on-dark-background issue, and the latter obscures the women's gowns with cloaks and bonnets with crowns. I can better interpret the folds of her bonnet and veil on the copy of Elizabeth's effigy (Pietro Torrigiano, 1512-1518) on display on the National Portrait Gallery's front stairs. Although the original effigy is in Westminster Abbey, it is all but invisible behind a decorative metal screen.
Margaret Beaufort's portrait is also a late 16th century copy of an earlier work. Her headdress is different in both color (white instead of black) and shape (the back of the veil is curved and shaped like her head, not laid over a rigid undercap), from Elizabeth's because she was a vowess when it was painted. This is similar to the variation seen in other widows' veils, mostly depicted on brasses. It differs somewhat from the shape of bonnet that she wears on her effigy (Pietro Torrigiano circa 1514), which I photographed at Westminster Abbey.
The next queen of England, Catherine of Aragon, does not seem to be painted in the same style as her mother-in-law Elizabeth. She showed up in England wearing Spanish fashion (Michael Sittow 1502) and by the 1525-1526 miniature by Lucas Horenbout (or Hornebolte) she had adopted the English gable, but already wore it with the frontlet flipped up, not down on her chest. In this remarkably different 1525 Horenbout minature she wears neither the same gown style nor a similar bonnet to Elizabeth of York. In some ways this is not surprising, since more than 20 years had passed since Elizabeth's death. However, monumental brasses of the 1520s usually look quite like the former queen's portrait and almost never mimic the current queen's fashion.
Henry VIII's later wives only move further from the fashions of 1500, displaying rigid torso support, full sleeves, and French hoods in their portraits.
There does not seem to have been a portrait painter active in Henry VII's court; only his wife, mother, and sons are memorialized during this time. His mother-in-law Elizabeth Wydeville or Woodville, queen consort of Edward IV and mother of Elizabeth of York, was painted circa 1471. However, I know of no other surviving portraiture from 1475-1520 depicting English women. context:The speaker analyzes the scarcity and inaccuracy of early Tudor portraits compared to funerary art like brasses, explaining how the lack of contemporary visual records for figures like Elizabeth of York and Catherine of Aragon makes it difficult to determine the specific differences in their clothing styles. keywords: Elizabeth of York, Catherine of Aragon, Tudor fashion, portraiture, funerary art tags: tudor_fashion_documentation, visual_source_analysis, funerary_art_importance, early_tudor_portraiture_limitations, fashion_evolution, visual_analysis, tudor_portraiture, historical_fashion_details, 16th_century_fashion
